content.text:
**Very well as the underlying engine; it still needs an Omarchy-specific integration layer.** I found DHH’s [August 15 “Dots” plan](https://github.com/basecamp/omarchy/blob/quattro/plans/dots.md)—a design document, rather than a shipped implementation in the branches I inspected.

Its three central needs map directly onto the mise stack:

| DHH’s need | How mise addresses it |
|---|---|
| Preserve configs without moving files or introducing symlinks | `mode = "track"` keeps native files in place, with history in a separate bare repository. |
| Recover earlier settings | Checkpoints, per-file history/diffs, rollback, protective snapshots, and selective undo. |
| Make another machine feel like this one | Shared configuration streams, machine-local policies, conflict handling, and fresh-machine bootstrap. |

Those capabilities span [tracking #12849](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12849), [rollback #12835](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12835), and [sync/onboarding #12882](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12882).

The important remaining differences:

- **“What did the update change?” needs explicit integration.** Mise brackets its own bootstrap operations, but Omarchy migrations and refresh commands need labeled before/after saves. The watcher captures changes, but cannot reliably distinguish prior user edits from an update’s changes. `save --trigger update --description … --best-effort` provides the necessary building block. A convenient “diff the last update” surface would still help.
- **Omarchy’s audited file list is essential.** DHH deliberately excludes application state, tokens, nested repositories, and generated files. Mise supplies tracking/exclusion policies, but Omarchy must supply that curated configuration. Machine-specific files such as monitor settings should be tracked with `share = false`.
- **Publishing defaults differ substantially.** DHH explicitly wants manual “this setup is good” publishing. Mise defaults to automatic publishing and incoming application once connected. `settings.history.sync = "manual"` fits his intended behavior while retaining automatic local history.
- **History privacy needs a separate choice.** DHH keeps local snapshot history off the remote; mise also offers machine recovery uploads, with tracked files defaulting to `backup = true`. An Omarchy preset should use `backup = false` to match his plan, or explicitly offer encrypted backups.
- **The approachable product surface remains Omarchy’s job:** provisioning, existing-user migration, menu integration, reload commands, and handling existing Stow/chezmoi/yadm setups. Mise supports symlink-target tracking rather than implementing DHH’s blanket “stand down” policy.

Mise also goes beyond the plan: adaptive watching, explicit conflict resolution instead of falling back to remote contents, reversible pulls, platform/profile variants, and [encrypted sharing and recovery backups](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12895).

**My recommendation: use this stack to power `omarchy dots`, with a curated preset and thin command/menu wrappers.** The core capabilities are already there; the missing work is mostly defaults and lifecycle integration. I’d keep the first Omarchy experience local-first and manually published, as DHH specified. The stack remains experimental and unmerged; this was a source/design comparison, not an end-to-end Omarchy validation.
what should we improve on the mise side before launching?

I’d focus on making the existing behavior predictable and recoverable, rather than adding more features. Based on the stack review, these are my launch priorities:

1. **Separate automatic history from automatic sharing during onboarding.** Make `origin set` explicitly ask whether users want manual publishing or automatic synchronization, and clearly explain that automatic sync also writes incoming changes. Local autosave shouldn’t imply “my unfinished edits belong on every machine.”

2. **Make sharing and backup policies easy to understand.** `share = false` still permits remote backups. That distinction is useful, but easy to miss. Show a concrete preview grouped into **local only**, **shared**, and **remote backup**, including encryption status. Give users one obvious way to keep a file entirely local.

3. **Add a supported way to bracket external operations.** Something like:
   ```sh
   mise bootstrap dotfiles capture --label "omarchy update" -- omarchy-update
   ```
   It should record before/after checkpoints, retain the wrapped command’s exit status, and identify the pair even on failure. This would let distro updates, scripts, and agents participate without each implementing checkpoint coordination. Pair it with a convenient “show what this operation changed” command.

4. **Verify the complete recovery journey before launch.** One acceptance scenario should cover: two machines editing independently, offline changes, conflict resolution, an interrupted pull, undo, and recovery onto a fresh machine using an encrypted backup. The stack has substantial focused coverage; this checks whether those pieces form a usable recovery workflow, including credentials and keys.

5. **Tighten the first-run experience and documentation.** Tracking a file should make it unmistakable whether future edits are being saved automatically, and provide the exact next action if the watcher isn’t running. Fix contradictory wording in the branch docs—for example, “nothing leaves the machine” needs qualification once origins are discussed—and put experimental status prominently in the guides.

For the Omarchy use case specifically, **external-operation capture is the biggest capability improvement**. The curated file list, menu wrappers, and distro-specific defaults belong in Omarchy.

I’d defer additional sync modes, broader machine-state rollback, and more encryption features. The launch promise should be easy to demonstrate: **edit files normally, see what changed, recover confidently, and know exactly what leaves your machine.**

content.text: The capture command will record an external command’s exit result and a linked before/after pair, including failed runs. Operation diffs will use that recorded pair, so intervening saves won’t change what they compare. It will describe changes during the interval—not claim to reverse packages or other system effects.
